name: Montpellier Green
lede: Montpellier green is a name for verdigris, the green made from copper, taken from the French city that was an important verdigris-making center for several centuries.

sections.title: Verdigris by another name
sections.body:
Montpellier green is a name for verdigris, the copper acetate pigment [1][2]. The Dictionary of Colour tells the reader to look under verdigris, and lists it with other copper greens such as Scheele's green, chrysocolla, mineral green and verditer [1][3]. Verdigris itself, the blue-green that forms on copper, brass and ancient bronze, is said to come from the French for 'green of Greece' [1].

The swatch, #649688, is a muted blue-green [4]. Close relatives in our names are [[viridian]], [[emerald-green]] and [[bronze-green]] [4].

sections.title: A city and its wine
sections.body:
Montpellier was an important center of verdigris manufacture from the twelfth to the eighteenth centuries [2]. The trade was a by-product of the wine industry; the process used wine lees with plates of copper [2]. Pomet, writing in 1694, held that the bulk of French verdigris, and some used abroad, came from Montpellier and its surroundings [2]. Sixteenth-century literature mentions Montpellier verdigris being imported to Amsterdam [2].

The books add a caution. Kühn points out that Montpellier green or Montpellier verdigris was used as a generic term and did not always mean verdigris made in the Montpellier region [2]. South-east France, especially the Rhone Valley, was known for verdigris as a wine by-product [5].

sections.title: A copper green and its family
sections.body:
In the Dictionary's own words, copper green is a generic name for green pigments made from copper [3]. Copper resinate, introduced in the fifteenth century, was made from verdigris [3]. Compare [[malachite]], the mineral form of copper green.

What the books do not give is a single fixed hue. The sources give no fixed hue for the name, so the swatch is a modern approximation [2][4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Ridgway listed Montpellier green in 1912, the earliest color record in our sources [4]. In our archive the match is present in 91 paintings, 0.38 percent of 23,781, as photographed [4]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 14 of 1,674 paintings, about 4.3 times the expected rate [4]. The earliest match is a 1475 Botticelli, but the archive's early centuries are thin [4]. It is most over-represented in France, at 2.1 times expected [4]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color [4].

issues: Lede overstated 'much of Europe's supply'; 'sour wine and grape residue' corrected to wine lees; removed unsupported 'one of the first, from antiquity' and 'blue-greens to deeper greens'; fixed note 5 locator; opener attributed to Pomet
